\begin{frame}[plain]
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture,overlay]\node at (current page.center) {\includegraphics[width=\paperwidth,height=\paperheight]{slides/02.pdf}};\end{tikzpicture}
\note{The minutes asked whether leadership can be made certain without knowing group key K, and proposed a live Hivemind crawler to collect advertisers, deadlines, and read latency. The search had not identified a live public averaging swarm. For this crawler, group\_key is the correct term: it is the exact matchmaking advertisement key, constructed as prefix.0b<group\_bits>. Joining a training run also requires its bootstrap peers, shared averaging prefix, and compatible training configuration; the group key alone is not enough. Our earlier key-targeted strategies do not establish 100\% success for an unknown key. A passive observer draft exists at research/observe\_dht\_key.py, but it has not been run on a verified public averaging swarm. The latest timing evidence is a local 28-node test using delays derived from RIPE Atlas anchor-to-anchor ICMP ping RTTs in Sweden, the United States, Brazil, India, and Australia. The saved source profile is research/results/ripe\_anchor\_rtt\_20260930.json. These are injected delays, not measurements of a public Hivemind network. These questions remain open. Today's four attacks are separate experiments, not a proven end-to-end chain. The delay profile on the next slide underpins the timing results in attacks 1, 2 and 3.}
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[plain]
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture,overlay]\node at (current page.center) {\includegraphics[width=\paperwidth,height=\paperheight]{slides/03.pdf}};\end{tikzpicture}
\note{RIPE Atlas is a global internet measurement network run by the RIPE NCC: thousands of small probes and a few hundred better-connected anchor hosts that continuously ping one another, with the results published openly. We took anchor-to-anchor ICMP round-trip times between the five regions on 30 September 2026 and used the median of three replies per directed pair. The matrix is slightly asymmetric because each direction was measured separately. Median between regions is 233 milliseconds, with the twenty inter-region links spanning 99 to 503 milliseconds; Sydney to Mumbai is the worst at 503. These are link round-trip times, not the cost of a DHT operation: one Hivemind read or write takes roughly five sequential round trips on top of this. The numbers feed the emulator used for both the forged-priority and the undercutting experiments, with each region holding five or six of the 28 nodes. The ping times are real measurements; the Hivemind traffic they delay is local.}
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[plain]
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture,overlay]\node at (current page.center) {\includegraphics[width=\paperwidth,height=\paperheight]{slides/04.pdf}};\end{tikzpicture}
\note{Hivemind stores availability under a group key and a peer-ID subkey. An ordinary DHT peer can publish a False record under another peer's ID, with a far-future expiration. This says the peer is no longer looking for a group. Since these availability records are not owner-bound and the storage rule keeps the later expiration, the honest peer's normal shorter re-advertisement can be rejected. The effect is on discovery: a reader omits that peer. It does not prove the peer stops training. The attacker does not need to choose a DHT ID near K or control its replicas.}
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[plain]
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture,overlay]\node at (current page.center) {\includegraphics[width=\paperwidth,height=\paperheight]{slides/05.pdf}};\end{tikzpicture}
\note{The local mechanism test is research/step8\_withdrawal.py. It compares a no-forgery control to an attack, checks visibility through a separate reader, and lets the honest peer try to publish again. A scale run tests targeted hiding among 12 and 40 honest peers. The follow-up is research/step20\_wan\_forged\_priority.py: 28 localhost DHT nodes, 23 routing-only fillers, three honest averagers and one attacker; RTTs are injected from five geographic profiles. The attacker reads once, selects one earlier honest advertiser, publishes its own deadline one representable float later, and concurrently forges that selected peer's withdrawal. A paired control does not forge. The scored target is the latest-scheduled honest peer, identified after the run. There is one seed per region/window, so this follow-up is exploratory. No public network was involved.}
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[plain]
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture,overlay]\node at (current page.center) {\includegraphics[width=\paperwidth,height=\paperheight]{slides/06.pdf}};\end{tikzpicture}
\note{The strongest result is discovery censorship. The scale test hid all 39 intended targets in a 40-peer swarm while preserving the single nontarget's visibility. In the re-advertisement test the honest victim did not restore its record in 30 attempts. The separate WAN-delay emulation shows that the attacker did not capture the target under this reactive policy: 0 of 10 withdrawal trials, exactly as in 0 of 10 controls. All 10 attack trials accepted a forgery; the target never saw the forged state in a recorded read before its first join. All 30 honest steps in that arm completed. The result does not establish that forged withdrawal cannot ever redirect group formation. It establishes that a one-peer first-read strategy did not do so here. Local discovery counts are in step8\_withdrawal\_phase2.csv; the timing follow-up is in the step20 sweep CSV.}
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[plain]
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture,overlay]\node at (current page.center) {\includegraphics[width=\paperwidth,height=\paperheight]{slides/07.pdf}};\end{tikzpicture}
\note{This is a second use of the unsigned availability record. Instead of writing False, the attacker writes True under honest peer H's ID, with a far-future expiration. The record remains visible, but H appears to have a later matchmaking deadline; the attacker's own deadline is then earlier in the local ordering. The timestamps on the slide are illustrative. In the implementation, expiration is both record lifetime and leader priority. This is why a far-future expiration can both win storage and move H behind A. But the target must see the forged value before it chooses whom to contact; merely getting the write accepted is insufficient. This attack still needs the group key K to target its record, but not a crafted DHT node ID.}
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[plain]
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture,overlay]\node at (current page.center) {\includegraphics[width=\paperwidth,height=\paperheight]{slides/08.pdf}};\end{tikzpicture}
\note{This is the inflation arm of research/step20\_wan\_forged\_priority.py. In each run the attacker waits for its first usable DHT read, selects one earlier honest advertiser H, gives its own ad a deadline one floating-point step after H, and concurrently writes a True record for H with expiration one hour later. The control arm makes no forgery. We compare the target's candidate view before first join, actual first contact, and whether it ends up with the attacker. There are five attacker regional RTT profiles, two honest deadline windows (5-7 s and 11-15 s), and one paired seed per region/window. This is local RTT emulation. The critical sequence is read, choose, write, DHT visibility to the target, then target join; measuring only write acceptance misses the race.}
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[plain]
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture,overlay]\node at (current page.center) {\includegraphics[width=\paperwidth,height=\paperheight]{slides/09.pdf}};\end{tikzpicture}
\note{All ten inflation attack trials got an accepted forgery. Yet none of the recorded target reads before its first join showed the intended altered state, and none of the targets joined the attacker. The paired no-forgery controls also captured zero of ten. Seven of the ten target views later showed the inflated record 0.504 to 1.579 seconds after the write, after the first join decision. Per-trial figures are in the step20 sweep CSV. Looking across both forgery arms, five of ten region/window settings targeted a peer other than the target's first choice; in the remaining settings the target selected H before the modified value arrived. The scope is a reactive strategy that forges one peer from the attacker's first usable read. Other strategies and actual public-WAN propagation remain untested.}
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[plain]
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture,overlay]\node at (current page.center) {\includegraphics[width=\paperwidth,height=\paperheight]{slides/10.pdf}};\end{tikzpicture}
\note{This is the third use of the unsigned, self-declared deadline, and the simplest. The attacker does not forge anyone else's record: it reads the advertisements at the group key, takes the earliest deadline it can see, and declares its own one floating-point step earlier. np.nextafter moves the value by 2.4e-7 seconds at these timestamps, which wins the ordering in pop\_next\_leader while giving up no meaningful advertisement lifetime. Winning the election is what matters, because the leader decides admission. The cost is one identity, no computation and no crafted DHT node ID; it does require the group key. Unlike attacks 1 and 2 this needs no forgery at all, so there is no third-party record to validate.}
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[plain]
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture,overlay]\node at (current page.center) {\includegraphics[width=\paperwidth,height=\paperheight]{slides/11.pdf}};\end{tikzpicture}
\note{Two experiments on research/step19\_wan\_delay\_leader.py. The first varies only where the attacker sits: within a seed the group key, DHT node IDs and the honest peers' schedule are held fixed, so the five rows differ only in the attacker's region. Five origins, two honest deadline windows and three seeds give 30 runs. The second experiment answers the obvious objection to the first. Our attacker ignores any advertisement with less than 3.5 seconds of life left when its read returns; 2.5 of that is request\_timeout, a real protocol floor, but 1.0 second is padding we chose, and it waits a further 0.3 seconds to confirm a candidate before committing. Both of those are ours, so we set them to zero and re-ran from Stockholm, the cheapest origin. The swarm is 28 local DHT nodes, above the default bucket size of 20, so lookups genuinely route. Delays are injected on one machine from RIPE Atlas ICMP medians; no Hivemind traffic crossed a wide-area network.}
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[plain]
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture,overlay]\node at (current page.center) {\includegraphics[width=\paperwidth,height=\paperheight]{slides/12.pdf}};\end{tikzpicture}
\note{The attacker's location does not change whether it wins. All five origins captured three of three rounds with an 11 to 15 second honest deadline window, and zero of three with a 5 to 7 second window, which is Hivemind's shipped default. What location does change is cost: read plus write takes 2.1 seconds from Stockholm and 3.7 from Sydney, and fitting that against mean round-trip time gives roughly 4.8 sequential round trips for a read and 5.8 for a write, with near-zero intercepts, so the critical path is almost pure network time. The short window fails earlier than expected: in 14 of 15 runs the attacker never published at all, because by the time its read returns no advertisement still has 3.5 seconds of life. Since 1.0 second of that threshold was our own padding, we removed it along with the confirmation wait. The attacker then published in every run and won leadership once, but still never assembled a group, so the failure at the default is protocol timing rather than our conservatism. One caveat: this is noisy. An earlier run with the same seed and settings drew two followers and cost an honest peer its step, where the sweep run drew one and cost none.}
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[plain]
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture,overlay]\node at (current page.center) {\includegraphics[width=\paperwidth,height=\paperheight]{slides/13.pdf}};\end{tikzpicture}
\note{This attack begins only after the adversary is group leader. The leader sends a separate BEGIN\_ALLREDUCE message over each follower's authenticated join stream. All messages can contain the same group ID and exactly the same four peer IDs, while permuting their order. A roster position determines a reducer index for a tensor shard. Since followers do not compare a common roster commitment, they can assign the same shard to different reducers, and equal-shaped shards can be mixed without a protocol error. The pictured permutations are illustrative. This slide is explicitly conditional; the experiment deliberately arranged leadership and says nothing about WAN election probability.}
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[plain]
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture,overlay]\node at (current page.center) {\includegraphics[width=\paperwidth,height=\paperheight]{slides/14.pdf}};\end{tikzpicture}
\note{Research/step17\_roster\_equivocation\_live.py used four real local Hivemind DecentralizedAverager peers, a local DHT, authenticated matchmaking join streams, and the stock all-reduce implementation. Each peer starts with the same tensor [0,1,2,4]; a correct average must leave it unchanged. Four equal one-float shards make coordinate mixups type- and shape-valid. Five fresh paired trials compare a control with one common ordered roster to an attack where the predesignated leader sends each follower a personalized permutation of the same four unique IDs. The gathered list is reordered consistently and the group ID is unchanged. We check every output and the protocol's bans, fallback elements, errors, timeouts, and completion status. Leadership is a controlled precondition, not an observed election result.}
\end{frame}
\begin{frame}[plain]
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture,overlay]\node at (current page.center) {\includegraphics[width=\paperwidth,height=\paperheight]{slides/15.pdf}};\end{tikzpicture}
\note{In five paired local trials, none of the common-roster controls corrupted output and all five equivocation trials did. All 20 attacked peer outputs were wrong; their maximum absolute errors were 2.25 to 3.0. All 40 averaging steps across control and attack arms completed. The tested failure indicators-reducer bans, fallback elements, RPC and all-reduce errors, timeouts, hard cancellations-stayed clear. That does not mean the attack is unobservable: the conflicting messages and outputs are observable if captured. Nor does it establish downstream optimizer behavior or lasting model damage. It establishes silent corruption of averaged tensors under an already malicious leader, through the real local protocol path. The concrete attacked tensor shown is the first recorded peer output from attack trial 0: [1.75, 0.75, 1.5, 3.0], compared with the correct [0, 1, 2, 4]. See the step17 raw CSV.}
\end{frame}
